titre: Magna Carta, Article 17: The Court That Stops Following the King
accroche: In 1215, the Great Charter orders that lawsuits between subjects be held in a fixed place, no longer wherever the king's court happens to be.
contenu_vulgarise:
On June 15, 1215, in the meadow of Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines, King John grants a charter to his barons. What people usually remember are the liberties and the judgment by peers. The charter runs to 63 articles in the Avalon Project's (Yale) translation. Article 17 is of a different nature: "Common pleas shall not follow our court, but shall be held in some fixed place." Lawsuits between subjects, which do not concern the king, will no longer follow the king's court: they will be held in a fixed place.

## A justice system on the move

To measure the clause's reach, one needs to know what the king's court was. According to Wikipedia's summary, the *curia regis* gathered the advisers and courtiers who followed the king on all his travels. It was not a specialized tribunal. When the king moved, his court moved with him. On the reading Wikipedia reports, the clause guarantees that there is a fixed place where plaintiffs and defendants can go, instead of a justice system that travels like the king.

The following article does the opposite for three kinds of inquiries into land possession (*novel disseisin*, *mort d'ancestor*, *darrein presentment*). The king will send two justices to each county four times a year, and these inquiries will be held in the county court. The same charter thus fixes one court in place while sending judges on the road for other matters.

## A court tied to a place

The Court of Common Pleas (or Common Bench) owes its address to this clause. Wikipedia describes it sitting at Westminster Hall, alongside the Exchequer of Pleas and the Court of King's Bench, and bound to sit there by Magna Carta. Wikipedia counts roughly six hundred years of existence for this court, and Sir Edward Coke held it to be the "lock and key of the common law."

The charter does not create the court, though. A 1178 decree of Henry II, which reduced to five the number of judges charged with hearing the kingdom's complaints, was first read as the founding of the Court of King's Bench, then, under a later theory, of the Court of Common Pleas. In the twentieth century, better equipped with documents, legal historians concluded that the court descends from the Exchequer of Pleas. The clause gives it a place, not an existence.

## What this shifts

The fixed place could be negotiated. According to Wikipedia, Richard II temporarily moved the court to York, in a dispute with the City of London. A seventeenth-century story, which Wikipedia judges apocryphal, claims the opposite: that Orlando Bridgeman refused to move the tribunal a few feet to avoid a draft from the north entrance, for fear of violating the Great Charter.

The Court of Common Pleas disappears in 1880. The English Supreme Court of Judicature Act of 1873 had merged the Westminster courts into a single High Court of Justice, and an Order in Council of December 16, 1880 ended the division of common pleas. The clause dates from 1215; the end of the Common Pleas division, from 1880.

A charter famous for what it forbids the king also settled a question of address: knowing where to go to plead, even before knowing what the judge will decide.

carte.punch: In 1215, the Great Charter orders that lawsuits between subjects stop following the king.
carte.idee: Article 17 of Magna Carta says that common pleas — lawsuits between subjects — will no longer follow the king's court, but will be held in a fixed place. The Court of Common Pleas then sat at Westminster Hall until 1880.

quiz.question: According to the 1215 Magna Carta (Article 18), where are inquiries into land possession such as novel disseisin held?
choix: In the county court, before two justices sent four times a year
In the fixed place set for common pleas, chosen by the king
In the king's court, which judges these inquiries wherever it is
Before the barons, gathered in their own lordships each year
quiz.explication: Article 18 provides that these inquiries be held in the county court, before two justices sent four times a year. The same charter thus fixes the common pleas in place (Article 17) and sends justices out to the counties for other matters: none of the other three answers is in the text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to twentieth-century legal historians, better equipped with documents, where does the Court of Common Pleas come from?
choix: From a 1178 decree of Henry II said to have founded it directly
From the Court of King's Bench, of which it would be a late split
From Magna Carta itself, said to have created it in 1215
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In the twentieth century, better equipped with documents, legal historians concluded that the court descends from the Exchequer of Pleas; the 1178 decree had first been read as founding the King's Bench, then the Common Pleas, before this later conclusion. Magna Carta does not create the court — it only gives it a fixed place.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Wikipedia, what does Richard II do with the Court of Common Pleas during a dispute with the City of London?
choix: He suppresses it temporarily, leaving no tribunal at all for common pleas
He temporarily moves it to York
He merges it with the Court of King's Bench
He hands it over to the justices sent out to the counties
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Wikipedia, Richard II temporarily moved the court to York, in a dispute with the City of London — a temporary move, not a suppression, a merger, or a transfer to the county justices.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What ends, in 1880, the division of common pleas within the Westminster courts?
choix: A direct repeal of Article 17 of Magna Carta by Parliament
The permanent move of the court to York decided under Richard II
An Order in Council of December 16, 1880, after the 1873 merger of the courts
The death of Sir Edward Coke, who presided over it
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Supreme Court of Judicature Act of 1873 merged the Westminster courts into a single High Court, and an Order in Council of December 16, 1880 ended the division of common pleas; none of the other three answers is in the text.
